title: Rare Earth Elements: Pathways to secure and diversified supply chains
date_evidence: IEA report 'Rare Earth Elements: Pathways to secure and diversified supply chains' was published on 8 April 2026 (IEA news release 'New projects, partnerships and policies are needed to address supply chain risks for rare earth elements'); page cite line reads 'IEA (2026), Rare Earth Elements, IEA, Paris'.
key_claim: China accounted for 91% of global refined rare-earth output and 94% of sintered permanent-magnet production in 2024; the October 2025 controls added a licence requirement covering any internationally made parts, components and assemblies containing Chinese-sourced rare earths or made using Chinese technology; if implemented in full the downstream production at risk reaches USD 6.5 trillion a year outside China, with the US and Europe each exposed to over USD 1.5 trillion; even with planned projects, ex-China capacity by 2035 meets only about 50% of mining, 25% of refining and well below 20% of magnet demand.
frame_summary: The IEA frames China's rare-earth dominance and the 2025 export controls as a systemic economic-security risk whose full implementation would put USD 6.5 trillion of downstream output at risk, and argues diversification requires a large, coordinated investment and preparedness effort.
verbatim_quote: If these rare earth export controls were implemented in full, the economic value of downstream production at risk would reach USD 6.5 trillion per year
verbatim_list: the country represented 91% of global refined output
its share expanded significantly to reach 94% in 2024

these controls included a new licence requirement covering the trade of any internationally made "parts, components and assemblies" containing Chinese-sourced rare earth materials or produced using Chinese technologies
The United States and Europe face the greatest exposure with potential direct economic losses estimated at over USD 1.5 trillion each
it accounts for about 50% of the demand for mining, 25% for refining and well below 20% for magnets
notes: Tier 1 multilateral. Report published 8 April 2026 to inform G7 discussions under the French Presidency; PDF versioned 4 May 2026. Anchors the quantification of concentration and downstream exposure and confirms the October 2025 parts/components/assemblies licence. title: Special report 04/2026: Critical raw materials for the energy transition
date_evidence: The European Court of Auditors published Special Report 04/2026 'Critical raw materials for the energy transition' on 2 February 2026; subtitle 'Not a rock-solid policy'; coverage (EUnews, 3 February 2026) records the auditors' finding that the 2030 targets 'appear out of reach'.
key_claim: The EU is 100% dependent on China for its supply of heavy rare earth elements; the auditors judge that the Critical Raw Materials Act's 2030 benchmarks for domestic extraction, processing and recycling appear out of reach, leaving the energy transition exposed to concentrated non-EU supply.
frame_summary: The EU's external auditor frames the bloc's critical-raw-materials policy as not rock-solid: dependence on China is a strategic vulnerability and the 2030 self-sufficiency targets are unlikely to be met on current trajectory.
notes: Tier 1 EU primary audit and the single structural anchor (3-6 month band; canonical primary source for the EU-exposure framing). Report page renders via JavaScript; publication date and headline findings confirmed via WebSearch snippet and multiple outlets (EUnews, S&P Global, Euronews) dated 2-4 February 2026. Cited in body as the EU-exposure anchor; no verbatim quote used to avoid provenance risk on a JS-rendered page.

title: Rare Earth Export Restrictions One Year Later
date_evidence: meta-citation_publication_date: Mon, 04/27/2026 - 12:00; visible byline 'Published April 27, 2026' by Gracelin Baskaran and Meredith Schwartz.
key_claim: One year after China's April 2025 restrictions, the October 2025 escalation included a strict foreign-direct-product rule preventing sale of foreign-made products with even trace amounts of Chinese-sourced rare earths without Chinese approval; the US has committed over USD 7.3 billion across five agencies and struck frameworks with Australia, Japan, Saudi Arabia and Malaysia, yet flows remain volatile and the DoD's 1 January 2027 ban on Chinese magnets may not be feasible on current capacity.
frame_summary: CSIS argues China remains an unreliable supplier even under the truce and that the unprecedented US whole-of-government response has bought distance but not yet displacement, so true resilience remains a multi-year execution challenge.

title: China's Critical Mineral Export Controls
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-04-29T21:07:46+00:00; visible dateline '04/29/2026'; by Haelim Anderson and Haotian Shi.
key_claim: China's Announcement 61 applies a 0.1% Chinese-origin content threshold to certain foreign-made items, mirroring the structural logic of the US Foreign Direct Product Rule but far stricter than the US 25% de minimis; China suspended the October 2025 measures for one year while leaving the April controls and the broader licensing architecture fully intact, and the March 2026 State Council Order No. 834 integrated export controls, data security and investment screening into a unified supply-chain-security framework, expanding scope even while extraterritorial enforcement stayed suspended.
frame_summary: Andersen Institute argues China has built a durable, flexible national-security export-control system that can be intensified, suspended or redirected without changing its legal foundations, and that its extraterritorial reach, though real, remains narrower and more administrative than the US direct-product rule.
verbatim_quote: China suspended the October rare-earth measures for one year while leaving the April controls and the broader licensing architecture fully intact
verbatim_list: China's Announcement 61 applies a far stricter 0.1 percent threshold to rare-earth content in certain foreign-made items
China's system remains narrower and more administrative than a full U.S.-style direct-product regime
the current equilibrium of mutual restraint is likely to hold, with selective pressure more probable than full escalation
notes: Tier 2 institutional. Anchors the 0.1%-vs-25% de minimis comparison, the FDPR-mirror framing, the 'suspended but intact' point and the March 2026 Order No. 834; also supplies the strongest counter-argument (regime narrower/more administrative; mutual restraint likely to hold). title: Recent China Export Control Actions Signal Active Enforcement for Rare Earths and Strategic Minerals
key_claim: On 24 June 2026 MOFCOM published Announcement No. 26 of 2026, effective 1 July 2026, formalizing a public reporting mechanism for strategic-mineral export-control violations, with reportable conduct including accepting foreign-government access or on-site verification requests without authorization; two Japanese nationals were detained in Dalian in May 2026 over alleged rare-earth smuggling; and companies are receiving significantly more detailed end-use and end-user due-diligence requests from Chinese exporters.
frame_summary: Morgan Lewis argues China's strategic-mineral export-control enforcement has become markedly more active, visible and extraterritorial in mid-2026, and that the compliance exposure now reaches any firm dealing in China-origin material regardless of where it is based.
verbatim_quote: The extraterritorial reach of its jurisdiction to anyone dealing in China-origin rare earth material means the compliance exposure is not limited to targeted companies.
verbatim_list: On June 24, 2026, MOFCOM published Announcement No. 26 of 2026, which formalizes the reporting and handling of violations involving strategic mineral dual-use export controls.
companies are receiving significantly more detailed end use and end user due diligence requests from Chinese exporters

title: China adds 10 US firms, including rare-earth miner, to export control list
date_evidence: meta-publishedDate: 2026-06-22T12:55:59; meta-lastDate: 2026-06-22T12:55:59; visible 'Published On 22 Jun 2026' by Erin Hale.
key_claim: On 22 June 2026 China's Ministry of Commerce added 10 US firms, including MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, to its export control list, barring foreign institutions and individuals worldwide from transferring Chinese dual-use goods to them; experts described the move as retaliation that is largely symbolic because the named firms had already cut Chinese supply, while cautioning there is 'no truce' in the trade war.
frame_summary: Al Jazeera reports the June 2026 entity listing as a tit-for-tat, largely symbolic escalation that nonetheless demonstrates the worldwide reach of China's dual-use export rules and the fragility of the post-summit truce.
